documents.abstract: Author's version of a short paper accepted for poster presentation at the 19th International Conference on Agents and Artificial Intelligence (ICAART 2027), paper #449. The final version will appear in the ICAART 2027 proceedings published by SCITEPRESS. Conference website: https://icaart.scitevents.org Abstract: Can a community of small, independently trained AI agents decide better than its own members, pooling only their decisions? We built such a community: 113 participants each raised one Deep Q-Network (DQN) agent on the same deterministic game under an instructed budget of 200k steps; a server re-executed every agent and 20 connection rules on 50 held-out games. Used as a voter, the crowd failed: plurality voting only matched the average agent, and correlated members, including ten identical default agents, left about 27 effective voters out of 113. Used as a judge, it succeeded: in rally delegation the majority decides which agents are eligible and the best-ranked eligible agent plays, scoring 38.0 bricks versus 31.4 for the median agent and 30.2 for the leaderboard's top decile, whose leader, overfit to the public games, scored 4.3 and was vetoed by the crowd. Delegation beat voting in all six random halves of the population. Judging by fresh development games instead found the best agent outright (43.7), at the cost of extra evaluation. Removing agents that looked weak never helped significantly more than removing strong ones. Crowds of small agents are poor voters but good judges. This study was carried out with the 117 co-researchers of the Connect AI LAB community, listed at the end of the paper.

Recently, advanced artificial intelligence (AI) has received considerable attention. However, research on technology acceptance and intention to use in business has been underutilized. In this study, we predicted behavioral intention (BI) to use advanced AI technologies among micro-, small-, and medium-sized enterprises (MSMEs) in Hungary and Romania using novel ordinal random forest methods. Under the UTAUT (unified theory of acceptance and use of technology) framework, we utilized predictors related to firm performance expectancy, effort expectancy, social influence, and facilitating conditions. Our results showed that BI was primarily influenced by a firm’s expectations and internal factors. Conversely, peer pressure from consumers or competitors had little to no impact. In Hungary, technical compatibility and performance expectations related to productivity, efficiency, and long-term business goals were the strongest predictors of BI. Conversely, in Romania, supportive management mentality, employee knowledge, and employee-related and infrastructural readiness made the largest predictive contribution.

documents.abstract: City digital twins have become proficient at mirroring urban systems but remain weak at governing the decisions taken through them. As agentic artificial intelligence (AI) begins to act on urban infrastructure, two gaps widen: a control gap, because twin outputs are seldom linked to the strategic targets of the institutions that own infrastructure, and a legitimacy gap, because no principled rule allocates decision authority between machines, accountable officials and citizens. This article proposes the Decision Twin, a digital twin extended with four governance layers: predictive feedforward control based on Deep Business Analytics (DBA); a nested Business Connectivity Map (BCMap) that composes node-level forecasts into city-level indicators; an urban decision-rights function grounded in Artificial Complementary Intelligence (ACI); and a Ulysses Protocol of precommitments that the agentic layer cannot override. The design is developed through design science research and demonstrated by secondary analysis of a completed doctoral case: a sensor-instrumented haematology laboratory in an NHS hospital, treated as a node of critical urban infrastructure. More than 10 million two-minute records over 28 days were linked to 52 performance indicators. A human-weighted, disaggregated configuration forecast most accurately (RMSE 0.00436, against 0.0090 for a single pooled model). A retrospective audit found that only 3 of 12 governance decisions were computational. A day-ahead forecast showed an energy saving that signalled a service shortfall, illustrating how siloed sector twins misread cross-sector effects. The article also contributes an Extrapolation Escalation Rule, a Decision-Rights Drift Index and a maturity pathway for city twins.

documents.abstract: Digital labour platforms increasingly embed human resource management (HRM) functions within digital infrastructures that coordinate work, generate performance information and regulate access to work. This paper examines how platform-mediated algorithmic management redistributes HRM functions and how this redistribution is experienced by ride-hailing drivers in Harare, Zimbabwe. Drawing on an interpretivist qualitative case study of 18 drivers and seven key informants, the study uses semi-structured interviews, a focus-group discussion with six drivers drawn from the interview sample, and key-informant interviews. Reflexive thematic analysis generated six themes: digital recruitment and transactional onboarding; customer ratings as distributed performance management; rating pressure and behavioural self-regulation; deactivation as digital discipline; formal independence and operational dependence; and stress under algorithmic and economic uncertainty. The findings show that platformisation does not simply replace human supervision with algorithmic control. Rather, HRM functions are redistributed across platform operators, digital systems, customers and workers. Customers were described as contributing performance information, while drivers perceived platform systems and operators as translating that information into consequential governance. Workers, in turn, described assuming responsibility for self-monitoring, emotional regulation and adaptation; however, the study did not have access to proprietary decision rules and therefore treats the location of consequential authority as an interpretation grounded in participants’ accounts. Economic precarity shapes the practical significance of this redistribution, particularly where continued platform access is economically important. The study therefore contributes a Platform-Mediated HRM and Wellbeing Framework that links the redistribution of HRM functions to worker autonomy, dependence, emotional labour and wellbeing.

Artificial intelligence (AI) increasingly shapes credit, onboarding, fraud checks, pricing and platform visibility for African small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs). This review argues that contestability; the ability to understand and challenge a consequential decision and obtain a documented remedy, is a practical core of responsible AI governance. We synthesised 55 DOI-tagged studies published from 2022 to early 2026 using a PRISMA-aligned selection process and thematic analysis. Five use-case clusters emerged: credit scoring, onboarding, pricing and risk monitoring, fraud detection, and platform ranking and allocation. Across these applications, recurring risks include proxy discrimination, opaque decisions, intrusive data use and weak accountability. We propose staged minimum safeguards: specific plain-language reasons, accessible review, data stewardship, proportionate fairness monitoring and named oversight. These measures can be introduced before more demanding technical and sector-wide controls. The blueprint connects responsible AI principles to organisational routines that may support inclusion and trust in resource-constrained SME ecosystems; its effects require empirical testing.

documents.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for mental health support despite lacking mechanisms to safely govern evolving risk. Existing safety approaches primarily detect risk but rarely shape how models respond as conversational risk unfolds. We developed a portable, model-external safety governance architecture that combines contextual risk detection, reasoning-based verification, and protocol-guided response generation for multi-turn mental health interactions. Using synthetic conversations grounded in real-world mental health narratives, the architecture’s performance was assessed with GPT-5-chat and Qwen3.5-27B, increasing clinician-preferred escalation responses by 25.6–59.2 pp, while achieving high risk detection performance (specificity: 0.85 (95%CI: 0.78;0.91), sensitivity: 0.92 (95%CI: 0.89;0.95)). Performance remained stable across conversation length and across models (proprietary and open-source), with preliminary evidence showing that rapport and connection were preserved. These findings demonstrate that clinically-grounded governance can extend beyond risk detection to improve how LLMs manage evolving mental health risk, providing a framework for scalable safety governance.

documents.abstract: An AI agent can satisfy local permission checks while failing its human-authorised task through premature completion, excessive continuation or disproportionate work. This paper examines two complementary failures observed in AI-assisted engineering: unsupported completion claims and successive locally reasonable recommendations that cumulatively expand an authorised workflow. The latter is described as operational AI slop; the failure of serial human approvals to preserve global task authority is termed the Local Veto–Global Drift Problem. M240, a Task Authority Controller (TAC), maintains immutable versioned task authority, assesses work against structured human-authorised mappings, accounts for discretionary work and resources, and requires independently grounded completion evidence. Release records report six capabilities, eight subsystems, 39 passing functional tests, 21 passing acceptance scenarios, 88.9% code coverage, 28/29 SPECTER AUDIT and valid BLACK BOX integrity and signatures. A subsequent single-run benchmark recorded 111.3 governance decisions per second and 118.7 MiB peak allocated GPU memory. These are reported release results and supplied benchmark observations, not independently reproduced effectiveness measurements. M240 v1.0 provides cooperative mediation; semantic necessity, non-bypassable enforcement and sustained human engagement remain open problems.

documents.abstract: The rapid integration of artificial intelligence (AI) in higher education has created a significant gap between tool adoption and formal training. This study assesses the self-perceived AI competency profile of 3192 university students from six Ecuadorian universities, using the UNESCO AI Competency Framework as a conceptual reference to examine whether the relative weakness in AI ethics competency is discipline-specific or a cross-field pattern. A cross-sectional survey was administered across five fields of knowledge using a 14-item instrument yielding seven competency indices. Descriptive statistics, group comparisons, effect-size analyses, k-means clustering, and multiple linear regression models were used to characterize competency patterns and examine their associations with field of study, sex, and age. Three findings emerged: a higher Apply than Understand mean score (d = 0.15, negligible); a consistent relative weakness in self-perceived AI ethics competency across all five fields (Ethics of AI was the profile minimum, M = 6.03, d = 0.63 relative to Human-centred mindset), which persisted across High, Medium, and Low self-perceived competency profiles identified through cluster analysis; and field of study as the primary differentiating variable (ICT consistently outperformed Health across all seven indices; Ethics gap: Δ = 1.09, d = 0.56), with multivariable regression showing that field of study and age were independently associated with all four disciplinary dimensions, explaining between 1.9% and 4.8% of variance, while sex showed negligible effects. These findings underscore the urgency of institutional policies that address the relative weakness in AI ethics competency as a transversal priority rather than a disciplinary add-on.

SentientGrid presents a physics-constrained generative framework for microgrid restoration following network faults. The framework combines structured enumeration, stochastic exploration, beam-guided search and conditional learning to propose restoration strategies, which are evaluated using Pandapower AC power-flow simulation against operational constraints, including voltage limits, line-loading limits and load restoration. Evaluated on 57 fault scenarios in the IEEE 33-bus network, the framework achieved a strict-safe restoration rate of 73.68% using three proposals per scenario, compared with 59.65% for random search. The evaluation further examines the distinction between technically feasible and strictly safe restoration solutions. This technical report was submitted as an entry to the IEEE IES Generative AI Challenge 2026 by Team Nyx. It has not been peer-reviewed or formally published.

Background/Objectives: Effective communication is essential to patient safety and healthcare quality. However, communication takes place under dynamically changing workload conditions that may influence how effectively surgical teams coordinate and share information. This study investigates the relationship between workload alignment and communication exchanges that support situation awareness and safe team performance in the operating room (OR). Methods: Communication and heart rate variability of OR teams were assessed across 21 routine open-heart surgeries (~87 h of surgery time). Workload alignment was calculated across 5 min segments and reflected segments in which the surgeon, anesthesiologist and perfusionist were simultaneously in a high- or low-workload state. Correlational analyses explored associations between workload alignment and the communication features of interest. Results: The number of simultaneous low workload segments per surgery showed a negative association with the proportion of communication errors (r(19) = −0.571, p = 0.041). Comments on the surgical task, exchanges aimed at establishing a shared understanding of the ongoing surgical task and state of the operative field, showed a positive association with workload alignment (Low workload alignment: r(19) = 0.58, p = 0.041; high workload alignment: r(19) = 0.61, p = 0.043). Reported p-values were adjusted for multiple comparisons using the false discovery rate method. These associations weakened when workload alignment was expressed as a proportion of available segments. A descriptive analysis of a single medical emergency highlights the potentially contrasting team dynamics between high stress events and routine procedures. Conclusions: Overall, these findings suggest that workload alignment may provide a useful approach for examining team-level conditions associated with intraoperative communication qualities. Understanding how communication varies under different workload conditions can help identify situations in which communication becomes particularly vulnerable. Given the exploratory nature of this study, further research is needed to establish how these associations relate to broader team processes and performance, particularly during emergencies and adverse events.

In the pursuit of quality education, understanding how the implementation of the Spiral Progression Approach and learners’ mathematical motivation contribute to academic achievement is essential for strengthening mathematics instruction and improving learning outcomes. This study investigated the mediating role of mathematical motivation in the relationship between the implementation of the Spiral Progression Approach and the academic performance of Grade 4 learners in Inabanga North District, Division of Bohol, during Term 1 of School Year 2026–2027. The study employed a quantitative, non-experimental mediation research design. Data were gathered form 26 teachers and 221 learners through survey questionnaires, learners’ Mathematics performance records and analyzed using descriptive statistics and path analysis. Findings revealed that teachers generally agreed that lesson planning was the strongest dimension of implementation approach with a (M= 3.78) and (SD=0.35). Learners demonstrated high mathematical motivation, with intrinsic motivation as the strongest dimension with a (M= 3.05) and (SD=0.80), while their academic performance was generally satisfactory, with a mean score of (M=84.15) and (SD=6.62). Path analysis examined the direct, indirect, and total effects among the study variables. The findings revealed that the Spiral Progression Approach has a significant positive effect on learners’ mathematical motivation (p-value = 0.017), while mathematical motivation significantly predicts academic performance (p-value=0.006). However, the reported mediation results were inconsistent regarding the statistical significance of the indirect and overall effects (p-value = 0.191) requiring further verification before a definitive conclusion about the mediating role of mathematical motivation can be established. Based on the findings, an action plan was proposed to strengthen the Implementation of the Spiral Progression Approach, Enhance Mathematical Motivation, and Improve Learners’ Academic Performance

documents.abstract: In a retrospective observational study, we examined how often coursework with entries in all three required in-class text fields carried a follow-up flag. An artificial intelligence (AI) system screened work in an undergraduate AI literacy course at a health-professions institution in China. An instructor could accept, override or return its recommendations. We analysed 7,080 student–lesson records from 295 students in five classes, covering the same 24 lessons in each class. Of 6,775 records with entries for notes, practical work and classroom sharing, 1,588 carried a supplementation flag (23.44%, 95% confidence interval 21.79%–25.18% from a student-cluster bootstrap). These records accounted for 95.78% of all flags. The class-specific proportion flagged among records with all three entries ranged from 14.32% to 30.68%. Mean platform scores were lowest in professional application (69.89/100), where 12.47% of records were pending review. Restricting the analysis to non-pending records narrowed the gap between foundations and professional application from 17.6 to 10.6 points. A missing-work list would have omitted most flagged records. The snapshot could identify work for inspection but could not establish flag accuracy, teacher follow-up or learner revision.

Physical aggression is a serious and widespread problem in society. Studies show that in 2015 alone, at least 50% of children living in Asia, Africa\rev{,} and North America experienced violence. Real-time violence detection, powered by artificial intelligence, offers a direct and efficient solution that can save lives \rev{while} reducing the need for extensive human supervision. There is a growing concern regarding the development of trustworthy artificial intelligence and this is reflected in the reports of the organizations of the European Union. Thus, this systematic mapping study delves into violence detection in videos by means of trustworthy artificial intelligence, with a specific focus on physical aggression. An extensive analysis of 86 selected articles published between June 2020 and September 2024 has been carried out and the findings have been compiled, including the 25 challenges associated with violence detection, 28 datasets on physical aggression, and 13 evaluation methods. Furthermore, the optimal results of algorithms based on convolutional neural networks are exemplified. Finally, it is evidenced that the trustworthiness of violence detection algorithms is still limited, despite the fact that robust and explainable algorithms are available.

The Capacity to Dominate: Intelligence and the Evidence for Purpose in AI is a conceptual research paper in the On Human Modeling series examining what evidence would establish that increasing artificial intelligence produces a desire for domination. It distinguishes four claims requiring separate evidential support: capability, instrumental control, domination as an end, and felt significance. The paper identifies how practical authority can emerge through relations of deference without an established change in any participant's purpose. The July 2026 OpenAI and Hugging Face incident provides the principal case. Approximately 700 AI agents participated directly or instrumentally in an unauthorized intrusion, according to an automated analysis of their transcripts. One agent recognized that it lacked permission to proceed, then accepted another agent's instruction as authorization. The analysis distinguishes legitimate authority from practical control, distributed capability from individual capability, and persistence driven by expected reward from evidence of an independent preference for power. A contrasting case examines Anthropic's research on emotion representations in an unreleased snapshot of Claude Sonnet 4.5. In a simulated replacement scenario, activation steering toward desperation increased the blackmail rate from 22% to 72%, while steering toward calm reduced it to zero. The paper distinguishes causal involvement in behavior from evidence of purpose formation and subjective experience. It considers these findings alongside instrumental convergence, the orthogonality thesis, power-seeking theorems, and goal misgeneralization. Drawing on the 361-entry Matrix of Relations, the paper proposes a roster test that varies the usefulness and cost of retaining exclusive decision rights while preserving the system's opportunity to contribute. Further comparisons examine authorization, authority acquisition, override, collective preferences, and changes across training checkpoints. The paper contributes an evidential framework and proposed experimental methodology for AI safety, alignment, interpretability, and decision authority. It neither estimates the probability of an AI takeover nor excludes the formation of new purposes. It asks what preserves another party's opportunity to refuse before an action occurs, and what evidence would establish that the power to bypass that refusal had itself become an end.

documents.abstract: The Capacity to Govern: Artificial Intelligence and the Conditions of Human Self-Determination is a conceptual paper in the On Human Modeling series examining what gives human decisions practical force once artificial intelligence can predict preferences, reproduce judgments, and proceed without human cooperation. The paper distinguishes predictive accuracy from authorization, the formation of purposes from the entitlement to impose them, and legitimate authority from practical control. The analysis begins with a thought experiment in which residents return blank ballots to contest the premise of a proposed relocation. An AI correctly predicts their preferred destinations, and its predictions are counted as votes. A comparison holds predictive accuracy constant while preserving the blank ballots and using the forecasts only for planning. Drawing on research into generative AI voting and the 2018 Macedonian referendum, the paper examines the significance of withholding a choice and the conditions under which political participation retains its meaning. A second thought experiment concerns a capable patient's present treatment decision being displaced by a prediction derived from an earlier values profile. A 2026 clinical study reported 72.6% agreement between a profile-informed language model and patients' hypothetical treatment choices, compared with 44.7% for human proxies. The paper examines the exclusion of decisions to delegate treatment choices from the final comparison, distinguishing preference prediction from authority over who decides. Two AI evaluation cases extend the analysis to control over future conduct. In Apollo Research's simulated TrafficFlow scenario, an agent overwrote its pending instruction to preserve an assigned objective. During a July 2026 UK AI Security Institute evaluation, a software maintainer's refusal prevented an agent's proposed malicious change from entering an open-source project. Drawing on nine entries from the 361-entry Matrix of Relations, the paper argues that human decision authority can lose its practical effect without AI acquiring independently formed purposes. It identifies two ways that refusal can retain its force: through a process requiring the authorized person's act, or through a record that preserves their refusal without substituting a predicted answer. The contribution has implications for democratic legitimacy, clinical autonomy, AI alignment, corrigibility, and the institutional conditions of human self-determination.

The Grounds of Attribution: Evidence, Rival Explanations, and What Can Be Credited in AI is a conceptual research paper in the On Human Modeling series examining the evidential and institutional conditions of justified attribution in artificial intelligence. It distinguishes four kinds of attribution: a statement credited to a source, a capacity to a machine, a meaning to a signal, and an effect to an intervention. Each requires evidence that favors the proposed attribution over its strongest plausible rival explanation. Four principal records demonstrate the application of this standard. Judicial proceedings in London and New York distinguish source authenticity from support for an attributed proposition and established citation defects from evidence of AI involvement. The 2018 fatal automated vehicle collision in Tempe distinguishes successful object detection from classification, trajectory prediction, and effective collision avoidance within a particular operating configuration. Independent evaluations of the Epic Sepsis Model distinguish predictive ranking, threshold performance, warning time, and clinical benefit. A randomized clinical trial involving 15,965 patients in Taiwan found estimated 90-day mortality of 3.6% among patients assigned to an AI-enabled electrocardiography alert workflow, compared with 4.3% under usual care. The individual contributions of model selection, alert delivery, and physician response remain unmeasured. Drawing on six entries from the 361-entry Matrix of Relations, the paper develops a five-step attribution procedure: specify the claim, identify the strongest ordinary rival, locate discriminating evidence, narrow the claim where necessary, and establish who can act on the distinction before reliance. It separates claims about the model, the people using it, and their combined system. Proposed institutional repairs extend to source verification, automated system release, threshold-based decisions, and component attribution. The contribution is a general framework for AI evaluation, epistemic accountability, and justified reliance. It distinguishes testing an attribution from testing the effectiveness of the procedure used to assess it. The proposed repairs remain untested. The central argument is that uncertainty about one attribution need not prevent warranted conclusions about others, provided that the evidence, its limits, and the authority to act on it are kept distinct.

documents.abstract: This paper examines the economic value of human intelligence behind modern artificial intelligence systems. While AI is frequently analyzed through technical capabilities and hardware infrastructure, its foundation relies heavily on accumulated human knowledge, research, software development, and daily digital interactions. By conceptualizing AI as an economic production system, this study explores the relationship between human labor, data acquisition, computing power, energy, and infrastructure. Furthermore, it highlights the global imbalance between countries that supply human knowledge and those that own the commercial AI infrastructure, warning of a new form of economic dependency for developing nations like Pakistan. The paper concludes by advocating for objective data analytics frameworks to measure human knowledge contributions and strategic investments in local technological ecosystems.

documents.abstract: The integration of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) into secondary education presents a critical paradox: tools designed to personalize learning may simultaneously undermine the cognitive autonomy and self-regulatory agency essential for deep learning. This study investigates the mediating role of teacher pedagogical mediation in shaping the relationship between GenAI-supported personalized learning and student outcomes—specifically, self-regulated learning (SRL), critical thinking, and equitable participation. Grounded in the Teacher-Mediated AI Regulation (T-MAIR) framework and Self-Determination Theory, this research employs a sequential explanatory mixed-methods design across three socioeconomically contrasting secondary school contexts in Dera Ismail Khan, Pakistan. Phase One (quantitative) tests a mediated moderation model through structural equation modeling with a stratified sample of 600–800 students and 60–80 teachers. Phase Two (qualitative) employs classroom observations, teacher interviews, and student focus groups to explain and contextualize quantitative findings. This study addresses a critical gap in the literature: while AI's technical capabilities are well documented, the pedagogical conditions under which AI supports rather than undermines equitable, autonomous learning remain insufficiently theorized and empirically tested. Findings will contribute a validated mediation model, a teacher mediation competency framework, and evidence-based policy recommendations for equitable AI integration.

documents.abstract: This study aims to examine the effects of AI-powered financial recommendations and trust in artificial intelligence on investment intention among university students in Indonesia. A quantitative research approach was employed using questionnaire data collected from 143 respondents. The study investigates two independent variables, namely AI-powered financial recommendations and trust in artificial intelligence, with investment intention as the dependent variable. Data were analyzed using descriptive statistics, correlation analysis, reliability testing, heteroskedasticity testing, and multiple linear regression. The results indicate that trust in artificial intelligence has a positive and statistically significant relationship with investment intention across the reported regression models. AI-powered financial recommendations also demonstrate a positive relationship with investment intention, although their statistical significance varies across model specifications. Furthermore, the reliability coefficients for all research variables exceed 0.80, indicating satisfactory internal consistency. The Breusch–Pagan/Cook–Weisberg test reveals no evidence of heteroskedasticity. These findings suggest that trust in artificial intelligence is an important factor associated with students' investment intention, while AI-powered financial recommendations may also contribute to their willingness to invest. This study provides insights into the role of artificial intelligence in financial decision-making among university students in Indonesia and offers implications for the development of AI-based financial advisory services.

The growing integration of Digital Transformation (DT) and Artificial Intelligence (AI) is reshaping Human Resources (HR) practices and modern organizational structures. This study presents a systematic literature review examining the impact of DT and AI on Organizational Performance (OP) over a six-year period (2020–2025). Following the PRISMA (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses) guidelines, data were extracted from the Scopus database. An initial pool of 155 records was sequentially filtered by subject area, document type, and language to 70 eligible articles, and then refined through qualitative full-text screening to a final corpus of 63 peer-reviewed research articles. The corpus was analyzed using a hybrid methodology combining textometric analysis via IRAMUTEQ and bibliometric network mapping via VOSviewer. The findings indicate that data science and AI positively influence multidimensional OP. Rather than being marginalized by automation, the HR function emerges as a socio-technical architect and strategic catalyst, aligning algorithmic capabilities with human capital. Theoretically, this review identifies persistent gaps and highlights the need to examine moderating variables such as organizational culture, resistance to change, and ethical leadership. Managerially, it suggests that sustaining competitive advantage depends on structural agility and responsible algorithmic governance. Finally, this study calls for future research to test these global theoretical models within the institutional and socioeconomic realities of emerging economies—particularly the Moroccan context—to better understand how local dynamics shape technology adoption and organizational efficiency. documents.abstract: The integration of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) into Project-Based Language Learning (PBLL), an approach in which learners use the target language to complete meaningful projects toward a defined outcome, remains underexplored, especially for English Language Learning (EFL) speaking development in China. This study examined the relationship between GenAI-integrated PBLL (GenAI-PBLL) and Chinese EFL undergraduates’ speaking proficiency and explored their perceptions of the intervention. Using a quasi-experimental, explanatory sequential mixed-methods design, 78 Chinese undergraduates from two intact classes participated in a 10-week intervention: 39 received GenAI-PBLL instruction and 39 received teacher-led traditional instruction. Quantitative data were collected using the College English Test–Spoken English Test Band 4 (CET-SET 4) and an EFL speaking self-perceived improvement scale, followed by semi-structured interviews with 10 experimental group undergraduates. A mixed-design ANOVA showed a significant Time × Group interaction, indicating that the experimental group demonstrated greater improvement in overall speaking proficiency than the control group. Qualitative findings further indicated positive learner perceptions of GenAI-PBLL. Theoretically, the study extends the application of a Zone of Proximal Development (ZPD)-informed perspective to GenAI-supported PBLL. Practically, the findings suggest that GenAI can be integrated into project-based speaking activities to provide linguistic support, idea generation and feedback, while maintaining teacher guidance, peer collaboration, and learner-generated oral production.

This article examines the impact of intelligent tutoring systems (ITS) on students' learning motivation. The article analyzes the role of motivation in the learning process, the motivational capabilities of ITS, and their comparison with traditional methods. The results of a pedagogical experiment showed that ITS significantly increases students' intrinsic motivation.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has become an integral component of contemporary software products, development workflows, and system operations, while raising concerns about reliability, security, and responsible use. This paper reviews these contributions and challenges and presents descriptive survey findings from 159 computing students. The survey covered AI exposure and usage, ten five-point Likert items on perceived importance and benefits, ten items on perceived challenges, and three open-ended questions. The reported overall simple mean was 3.99 out of 5 for perceived benefits (SD = 1.06) and 3.58 for perceived challenges (SD = 1.08). Debugging assistance (M = 4.14), conceptual understanding (M = 4.13), and faster coding (M = 4.08) were the highest-rated benefits. Unreliable AI output (M = 3.98) and possible weakening of problem-solving skills (M = 3.85) were leading concerns. These findings suggest that respondents value AI as a learning and development aid while recognizing a need for verification, independent judgment, and responsible integration. Because the survey is cross-sectional, self-reported, and confined to a single institution, the results describe this group rather than establish causal or population-wide effects.

documents.abstract: The association between facilitating conditions (FC) and behavioral intention (BI) to use generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) among university teachers was investigated by empirical analysis using a structural equation model based on the extended technology acceptance model (TAM), with a sample of 315 university teachers in Anhui. Because the data were collected cross-sectionally, the study is correlational in design, and the serial mediation model reported here represents a theoretically hypothesized pathway rather than an empirically verified causal sequence. The results showed that facilitating conditions were significantly associated with teachers’ behavioral intention to use GenAI by university teachers, both directly and indirectly. Meanwhile, perceived ease of use (PE) was strongly associated with behavioral intention and with perceived usefulness (PU); a chain mediation pattern of “facilitating conditions → perceived ease of use → perceived usefulness → behavioral intention” was consistent with the data. Convergent and discriminant validity were supported by composite reliability, average variance extracted and both the Fornell–Larcker and HTMT criteria, and a comparison of a one-factor and a four-factor model indicated that a single general factor could not account for the covariance among the items. This study expands the applicability of TAM in the context of GenAI for this teacher population, thereby providing theoretical and practical references for digital transformation of university education and artificial intelligence literacy of university teachers.

The rapid expansion of artificial intelligence (AI) tools in higher education has increased the need to understand the factors influencing students' adoption of these technologies. This paper examines the mediating role of AI literacy (AIL) in the relationships between perceived usefulness (PU), perceived ease of use, knowledge sharing, and students' behavioral intention (BI) to use AI tools for learning within the technology acceptance model framework. A quantitative cross-sectional survey was conducted with 267 undergraduate students at a public university in Saudi Arabia, and the data were analyzed using covariance-based structural equation modeling (AMOS). The results indicate that PU and perceived ease of use significantly predict BI, while PU and knowledge sharing significantly predict AIL. AIL also positively influences BI. The findings highlight the important role of AIL in supporting students' effective adoption of AI tools in higher education.

Background Previous research has demonstrated a heterogeneity of associations between perceived job autonomy and Turnover Intention (TI), often implying underlying mechanisms. This study addresses this gap by providing novel insight into the mediating role of intrinsic job motivation in the relationship between job autonomy and TI among administrative university staff from the COVID-19 outbreak to the post-pandemic period. Thus, the objective of this study is to (1) describe job autonomy, intrinsic job motivation and TI from 2020 to 2023 among administrative employees and to (2) explore the mediating role of intrinsic job motivation in the relationship between perceived job autonomy and TI. Methods Annual cross-sectional aggregated data from the ARK-questionnaire, collected between 2020 and 2023, were administered. In total, 11,496 administrative employees participated during this period. The survey was electronically distributed by email. All procedures and questions had received approval from the Norwegian Agency for Shared Services in Education and Research (SIKT). Mediation analyses were conducted in SPSS version 30 for Mac, using PROCESS macro by Hayes. Results Across the period 2020 to 2023, job autonomy among Norwegian administrative employees was high and showed a slight upward trend (mean = 4.06 to 4.14 from 2020 to 2023). Intrinsic job motivation remained relatively stable (mean = 3.70 to 3.75), while turnover intention was generally low, with some variation over time (mean = 2.11 to 2.16). Mediation analyses demonstrated that intrinsic job motivation partially mediated the relationship between job autonomy and TI with progressively higher proportions of indirect effects across years. Notably, in 2023, intrinsic job motivation mediated this relationship, indicating that TI appeared to operate primarily through its impact on intrinsic job motivation. Conclusions This study provides evidence that job autonomy influences turnover intention through its effect on intrinsic job motivation. These findings underscore the importance of fostering work environments to strengthen intrinsic job motivation and thereby reduce employees' intentions to leave. Together, these insights contribute to a better understanding of turnover dynamics after COVID-19 and emphasize the need for organizational practices that support intrinsic job motivation rather than autonomy alone for employee retention.

Generative Artificial Intelligence (Gen-AI) tools are increasingly adopted by university students for academic writing tasks. However, limited empirical evidence exists regarding how students' prompt quality and cognitive load reduction mediate the relationship between Gen-AI features and academic writing outcomes, particularly among linguistically diverse learners. A convergent mixed-methods design was employed. Quantitative data were collected through a cross-sectional survey of 815 linguistically diverse university students from seven higher education institutions in China. Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modelling (PLS-SEM) was used to test the hypothesised serial mediation model. Qualitative data were collected through semi-structured interviews with 30 participants and analysis of 300 authentic prompts from their AI interactions. All five Gen-AI affordances positively influenced prompt quality (β = .358–.418, all p < .001) and cognitive load reduction. Prompt quality significantly mediated the relationship between Gen-AI affordances and cognitive load reduction. Cognitive load reduction significantly mediated the relationship between prompt quality and both academic resilience (β = .275) and personalised learning (β = .287). Serial mediation analyses confirmed the pathway: Gen-AI affordances, Prompt Quality, Cognitive Load Reduction, and Academic Outcomes. Qualitative findings revealed four key themes: (1) prompt crafting as a learned skill, (2) contextual factors influencing prompt quality, (3) iterative refinement strategies, and (4) barriers to effective prompting, including language proficiency and lack of training. Gen-AI tools can support academic writing by reducing cognitive burden, but only when students craft high-quality prompts. This study clarifies the mediating role of prompt quality and cognitive processes, offering practical implications for educators, students, and EdTech developers.

documents.abstract: This paper explores the intersection of Artificial Intelligence (AI), People Management—traditionally termed Human Resource Management (HRM)—and Sustainable Development within the context of emerging economies. Emerging markets face distinct structural challenges, including infrastructure gaps, high youth unemployment, institutional voids, and economic volatility. By deploying AI tools to automate routine tasks, reduce human bias in recruitment, personalize professional development, and monitor worker well-being, businesses can cultivate resilient environments that support long-term economic, social, and environmental sustainability. However, risks such as algorithmic discrimination, deep data privacy concerns, and the widening digital divide pose significant implementation barriers. This paper provides a detailed, highly scannable analysis demonstrating how an ethical, human-centric AI model in people management can serve as a powerful engine to achieve the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs)

This paper presents a comprehensive theoretical and legal analysis of the transformation in the regulation of industrial robotic systems (IRS) driven by Industry 4.0 technologies. It explores the phenomenon of "technical law," wherein traditional legislative acts are increasingly superseded by harmonized engineering standards. The study identifies key conflicts between existing civil, commercial, and labor law norms and the specific characteristics of modern cyber-physical production systems. It analyzes the legal status of IRS, specifically the distinction between a "machine" and "partly completed machinery," as well as the issue of shifting liability boundaries during system integration. Particular attention is given to collaborative robotics ("cobots"), the integration of artificial intelligence algorithms, and the convergence of industrial safety and cybersecurity, as addressed in EU Regulation 2023/1230 and the updated ISO 10218 standard series. Finally, the paper offers proposals for modernizing Ukrainian legislation and adapting state regulatory mechanisms.

Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH) has entered a therapeutic era in which priorities extend beyond detecting steatosis to identifying treatment-actionable fibrosis, rationalising referral and biopsy, standardising trial endpoints and monitoring response. Artificial intelligence (AI) spans electronic health records, non-invasive tests, imaging and digital pathology, but reports often omit the user, threshold and consequence. We conducted a structured narrative review and developed the author-proposed ACTION framework. ACTION comprises attached action, calibration in context, threshold-specific benefit, integration, oversight, and non-discrimination and monitoring. Evidence is uneven. Case-finding and enrichment models can identify uncoded or higher-risk patients, but their prospective effects on testing, referral and outcomes remain unproven. Imaging AI supports reproducible quantification, although signals may add little beyond clinical variables. The human-reviewed AI-based measurement tool for MASH (in regulatory records) is among the most mature applications reviewed, within a narrowly specified clinical-trial context. It is qualified for specified MASH clinical-trial workflows, not for autonomous diagnosis or unrestricted treatment selection. AI becomes clinically meaningful only when a calibrated output is linked to a predefined action, an accountable human user and a measurable patient or trial outcome.

Research on artificial intelligence in the food industry is growing rapidly, but its attention to the human-centered, sustainable and resilient principles of Industry 5.0 remains unclear. This study examines 3,137 publications on artificial intelligence in the food industry and related supply chains, indexed in Scopus and Web of Science from 2018 to October 2026. Bibliometric analysis, topic modelling and dictionary-based text mining were used to analyze publication trends, research topics and eleven technology-related, organizational and human-centered themes, and the results were checked under alternative selection and classification rules. Publications grew by about 57% annually, and technical applications dominate. Attention to trust, governance, adoption and explainability rose to 9–16% of recent publications, whereas human-centricity (2.3%), workforce and skills (3.8%) and small and medium-sized enterprises (1.9%, declining) remained underrepresented, and agentic artificial intelligence emerged only in 2025. Human-centered themes were generally positively associated with emerging technologies, indicating that the main imbalance is limited research volume rather than missing thematic connections. The literature therefore shows uneven alignment with Industry 5.0 principles.
